chapter: Race, pay and the color line
title: Guarantees and percentages; hit-record popularity with white crowds
summary: Flat pay with a contract split after hits; his popularity after 'When I Meet My Girl', girls mobbing him in Alexandria, and keeping business on the bandstand.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you always work with the club? Did you always work for a flat guarantee? Did you ever get a percentage of the tape? No, no percentage. The only time, you know, after I had hit records, records that would sell, and you would go out and play for, well, the booking agency would write a contract you would get.

Say, $5.50. $5.50. $5.50 was a good price for a recording office at that time. $5.50 and 50% over $1,100. See, so how they do, I make $5.50, the promoter would make $5.50, then we split the difference. Yeah. And I can remember Shell Booking Agency booking me in Shreveport, and that's the way the contract run. I think I made a few dollars over, yeah. Yeah. But you know what? This was white, not black, because this was on When I Meet My Girl. And you know, I was more popular up that way. You know what I was doing? Oh, I was popular. And you know how that started? We played, I played in Alexandria at the community center. And boy, we just packaged it out, white, and we broadcast on the radio. And I'll never forget this. I was playing in the head of Little White Girls right in front of the bandstand. And when I finished playing the bandstand, boy, them girls jump up on that bandstand, and they jammed me up in the corner. And the police had to come get me, because they had me in the corner, you know. And you know, autographs, secrets and things. But this had this white, prejudiced police who was trying to see if I was trying to make eyes at this little girl, was there, oh, because she came up and told me how much she loved my music, when I meet my girl and all this. And she was so happy that she was from New York, but she was going to school up there. She came up and, but you know, I have always been that when I play music, I go to play music, and not seek recreation. All my recreation camp after I knock off. When I'm on the bandstand, that's why I say that's why I had a, could always go back. I had a business to do was play music. Yeah. Not seek. And this is what I instilled in the band. I said, man, look, we are going to play music. I said, let's play music. Anything you want to do, do it after we off. No more, and this is what it was. That's why I got along with people everywhere. And it just was that maybe we showed that we were there for business. Now, I know some black musicians that's after white girls, strictly. And one band in particular, I didn't call that name, but they were strictly after. And they got popular in town, but they also had quite a few Indians in town. And I noticed because I heard something.
